claims.text: A targeted thermo-mechanical treatment that forms coherent nanoprecipitates can improve room-temperature tensile ductility without sacrificing, and potentially increasing, strength.
The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The dual-phase lamellar colonies provide high strength.
Limited ductility and brittleness arise from dislocation pile-ups at internal colony boundaries.
A single-step combined annealing/aging treatment can trigger coherent nanoprecipitation in the target eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Coherent δ-lamellae and fine γ″ particles have been produced in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing at a strain rate of approximately 5×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ is applicable after treatment.
Processing in an inert atmosphere is required or beneficial for producing the desired coherent precipitates.
Carefully controlled treatment temperatures and times can foster coherent precipitation.
The treatment will form finely dispersed coherent nanoprecipitates with lamellar and spheroidal morphologies.
The coherent nanoprecipitates will modify internal boundary structure and promote dislocation shearing.
Coherent precipitate interfaces enable dislocations to transmit across barriers instead of accumulating at phase boundaries.
The precipitates pin dislocations in a controlled manner and thereby reduce local stress concentrations.
Reduced local stress concentrations mitigate microcrack nucleation.
The shearability of the coherent precipitates maintains strain hardening and ductility.
The treated alloy will retain or increase its strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will exhibit a significant improvement in room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will reduce premature crack initiation by lowering local stress concentrations at coherent interfaces.
The hypothesis applies only when alloy chemistry and processing permit formation and stabilization of coherent nanoprecipitates.
The optimum treatment temperature, time, cooling rate, precipitate volume fraction, size, and coherence remain undetermined.

contradictions.description: The treatment is called a single-step thermo-mechanical treatment, but the specified intervention is a combined annealing/aging heat treatment with no mechanical-deformation step. Annealing and aging also imply distinct thermal stages unless explicitly integrated into one cycle.
The predicted outcome requires strength to be retained or increased, but the falsification rule does not clearly falsify the hypothesis when ductility improves at the cost of reduced strength.
